result: Augmin is vital for the formation of uniformly arranged parallel units consisting of sister kinetochore fibers connected by a bridging fiber. STED microscopy revealed that in control cells, midplane-crossing microtubules form nearly-parallel bridging fibers connecting sister k-fibers, whereas after HAUS6 or HAUS8 depletion, these microtubules become wavy, disordered, and less often form proper bridging fibers, instead forming complex arrangements between various k-fibers.
evaluation: Claims C2, C20-C26, and C81 are strongly supported by STED microscopy data presented in Figures 1 and related supplements. The visual evidence clearly demonstrates the structural differences between control and augmin-depleted cells, with quantitative measurements confirming the disruption of bridging fiber organization. The use of superresolution microscopy provides sufficient resolution to distinguish these structures.

result: Bridging fibers are predominantly generated through augmin-dependent nucleation. STED microscopy quantification revealed that HAUS6 depletion resulted in 68±8% reduction of bridging fiber signal intensity and 24±6% reduction of k-fiber signal intensity. Based on intensity measurements and electron tomography data showing k-fibers consist of 12.6±1.7 microtubules, bridging fibers in control cells consist of 3.8±0.4 microtubules, with 2.6±0.7 microtubules nucleated in an augmin-dependent manner.
evaluation: Claims C48, C5, C50-C54 are supported by quantitative STED microscopy measurements (Figure 3D-E) and calculations based on established electron tomography data (C49). The method is validated by showing astral microtubules consist of 1.0±0.1 microtubules (C51), consistent with expectations. The calculation approach is clearly described in Materials and Methods, and the differential effect on bridging fibers versus k-fibers is consistently demonstrated.

result: A significant portion of kinetochore pairs lack detectable bridging fibers after augmin depletion, with spatial heterogeneity in the spindle. 41±4% of all kinetochore pairs in HAUS6-depleted cells had no detectable bridging fibers, with 50±5% in the inner part of the spindle lacking bridging fibers compared to only 27±5% in the outer part. This complete absence of bridging fibers, especially in the inner spindle, resulted in specific reduction of interkinetochore distance.
evaluation: Claims C55, C56, and C6 are supported by quantitative analysis of STED images (Figure 3H) with clear definition of 'undetectable' bridging fibers as those with signal below background. The spatial analysis showing preferential loss in the inner spindle is consistent across multiple measurements and validated by independent methods (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The connection to interkinetochore distance is demonstrated in Figure 5.

result: Augmin depletion leads to increased segregation errors when the checkpoint is weakened. Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion resulted in 5.7±0.8 segregation errors per cell compared to 1.5±0.2 in Mad2 depletion alone. While the number of misaligned kinetochore pairs was similar in both conditions, they were much more likely to missegregate without HAUS6 (80±9% vs 20±13%). Lagging kinetochores were both more frequent (2.6±0.4 vs 0.8±0.2 per cell) and more likely to missegregate (45±6% vs 23±8%) in Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion.
evaluation: Claims C27-C31 and C47 are supported by quantitative live-cell imaging data (Figure 2B) with clear definitions of error types and appropriate sample sizes (N=31 Mad2-depleted cells, N=30 Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells). The statistical analysis is appropriate, and the use of Mad2 codepletion to bypass checkpoint delays is well-justified. The data clearly demonstrate both increased error frequency and reduced error correction capacity.

result: Lagging kinetochore pairs in augmin-depleted cells have reduced interkinetochore distance and increased tilt. In Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells, lagging kinetochore pairs had an interkinetochore distance of 0.89±0.03 µm (significantly smaller than 0.98±0.02 µm in error-free pairs) and a tilt of 19.7±1.6° (compared to 10.9±0.8° in error-free pairs). In contrast, Mad2-depleted cells showed no such differences. The tilt inversely correlated with interkinetochore distance in augmin depletion but not in control cells. Notably, 19±5% of lagging kinetochore pairs in Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells were in the inner spindle where disordered microtubules appeared.
evaluation: Claims C40-C44, C38-C39 are supported by quantitative measurements from live-cell imaging (Figure 2G-I, 2F) with appropriate statistical tests showing significant differences. The correlation analysis (C44) is properly performed and visualized. The spatial distribution analysis (C38-C39) connects the phenotype to the structural defects observed by STED microscopy. Sample sizes are adequate (N=30-31 cells with 120-124 kinetochore pairs).

result: Merotelic attachments were found in HAUS6-depleted cells, with kinetochores forming attachments with microtubules from the opposite side of the spindle while missing proper bridging fibers. Cold treatment combined with STED microscopy confirmed the true merotelic nature by removing midplane-crossing microtubules and preserving only kinetochore microtubules. These findings support that augmin-nucleated bridging fibers prevent merotelic attachments by creating a nearly parallel and highly bundled microtubule arrangement.
evaluation: Claims C45, C46, and C3 are supported by STED microscopy images (Figure 2J-K) showing merotelic attachments. The cold treatment validation (C46) is a well-established method (cited: DeLuca et al., 2006; Sacristan et al., 2018; Silkworth et al., 2012) that strengthens the conclusion. The mechanistic interpretation (C3) is reasonable given the structural data showing loss of parallel bridging fiber organization and the correlation with merotelic attachments.

result: Augmin-nucleated k-fibers are required to resolve segregation errors during anaphase. Both anaphase A and B were reduced following Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion. For misaligned kinetochores, the kinetochore closer to the proximal pole moved correctly in both conditions, but the kinetochore further away typically moved toward the distal pole in Mad2 depletion (correct segregation) versus away from it in Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion (missegregation). Since interkinetochore distance was similar for correctly and incorrectly segregating pairs, missegregation likely occurs due to k-fibers with fewer microtubules creating insufficient force.
evaluation: Claims C32-C37 and C4 are supported by detailed kinetochore tracking data (Figure 2C-E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-H) with appropriate controls. The inference that insufficient force from thinner k-fibers causes missegregation (C37, C4) is reasonable given: (1) similar interkinetochore distances between correctly and incorrectly segregating pairs (C36), (2) reduced anaphase A speed (C32), and (3) citations to previous work on k-fiber force generation (Dudka et al., 2018).

result: Augmin has a specific role in regulating interkinetochore tension through bridging fiber nucleation. The interkinetochore distance was smaller in the inner part of the spindle in augmin-depleted cells (where bridging fibers were most impaired) but not in control cells. Kinetochore pairs without bridging fibers had significantly smaller interkinetochore distance than those with bridging fibers. Multiple lines of evidence separate bridging fiber from k-fiber contributions: (1) interkinetochore distance correlated more strongly with bridging fiber than k-fiber intensity after augmin depletion, (2) no correlation with k-fiber intensity within groups with or without bridging fibers, and (3) when k-fiber intensity was matched, interkinetochore distance was larger with bridging fibers than without.
evaluation: Claims C69-C77 are supported by comprehensive quantitative analysis using multiple approaches to isolate the specific contribution of bridging fibers (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The experimental design cleverly controls for k-fiber effects by comparing subsets with matched k-fiber intensities (C76), strengthening the conclusion. The correlation analyses (C73-C75) are properly performed with appropriate statistical tests. Sample sizes are adequate (N=30 cells with 158-180 kinetochore pairs).

result: Augmin-depleted spindles contain fewer overlap bundles with altered spatial distribution. PRC1-GFP signal intensity was reduced by 55±4%, and the number of PRC1-labeled overlap bundles was almost halved (from 28±1 to 16±1 bundles). Augmin-depleted cells showed a barrel-like distribution with more overlap bundles at the spindle perimeter and fewer in the central part. However, DNA, kinetochores, and tubulin signal remained uniformly distributed throughout the spindle cross-section.
evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are supported by quantitative analysis of PRC1-GFP cells using end-on view imaging (Figure 4A-D). The barrel-like redistribution (C64) is clearly visualized and quantified. The uniform distribution of DNA, kinetochores, and tubulin (C65-C66) provides important context showing that the redistribution is specific to overlap bundles, not overall spindle organization. Results are consistent across RPE1 and HeLa cells.

result: The relative length of overlaps with respect to spindle length increased following augmin depletion. In RPE1 cells, this increased from 48±1% to 57±2%, with comparable increases in HeLa cells. Interestingly, spindles in RPE1 cells shortened following augmin depletion, while those in HeLa cells were longer, consistent with previous observations in other systems.
evaluation: Claims C68 and C67 are supported by quantitative measurements (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1J-M) with appropriate statistical analysis. The cell-type-specific differences in spindle length (C67) are acknowledged and consistent with cited previous work (Goshima et al., 2007; Petry et al., 2011). The increase in relative overlap length is consistent across both cell types despite different absolute spindle length changes.

result: Augmin depletion affects spindle shape and dynamics. K-fibers without bridging fibers had significantly larger radius of curvature than other bundle types, contributing to a diamond-like spindle shape. Poleward flux was significantly reduced in U2OS cells following augmin depletion, with both k-fibers and remaining bridging fibers slowed down. Bridging fibers fluxed faster than k-fibers in both control and augmin-depleted cells. In contrast, PRC1 depletion does not affect flux despite reducing bridging fibers.
evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by quantitative analysis of bundle curvature (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K), photoactivation experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L-M), and citations to recent speckle microscopy work (Risteski et al., 2022). The comparison with PRC1 depletion (C61) provides mechanistic insight, though the proposed explanation is speculative. The data on spindle shape (C57) is well-quantified with appropriate controls.

result: The authors propose a model where bridging fibers form by augmin-based nucleation of microtubules along existing microtubules, creating antiparallel overlaps that slide apart to generate pushing force. The bridging fiber works together with k-fibers to produce tension and maintain appropriate kinetochore orientation parallel to the spindle axis, thereby preventing merotelic attachments and ensuring mitotic fidelity.
evaluation: Claims C78-C80 represent the main model proposed by the authors, integrating multiple experimental findings. The model is well-supported by: (1) structural data showing augmin-dependent bridging fiber formation, (2) functional data showing effects on tension and kinetochore orientation, (3) observations of merotelic attachments when bridging fibers are absent, and (4) segregation error data. While some mechanistic details (e.g., force generation by sliding) are inferred rather than directly demonstrated, the overall model is consistent with all presented data and previous knowledge.

result: K-fibers are largely nucleated in an augmin-independent manner, at the centrosome or kinetochores and chromosomes. The same number of microtubules in bridging and k-fibers (approximately 2.6-3.0) was nucleated by augmin, but augmin-mediated nucleation becomes the predominant pathway for bridging fiber nucleation because there are fewer microtubules in the bridging fiber to begin with.
evaluation: Claims C82, C85, and C86 are supported by quantitative data showing differential effects on bridging fibers versus k-fibers (Figure 3D-E, 3G). The inference that k-fibers are largely augmin-independent (C82) is reasonable given the less severe reduction (24-37% vs 68%). The interpretation that augmin becomes predominant for bridging fibers due to their smaller size (C86) is a logical inference from the quantitative data, though the proposed mechanism of directional growth (C85) relies on citations to previous work.

result: Background on spindle architecture and augmin function. The mitotic spindle consists of three major classes of microtubules (k-fibers, midplane-crossing microtubules, and astral microtubules), with bridging fibers representing midplane-crossing microtubules laterally attached to sister k-fibers. Augmin is an eight-subunit complex that recruits γ-TuRC for microtubule nucleation, with nucleated microtubules growing at 0-30° angles and showing directional bias toward kinetochores. Augmin depletion results in multiple spindle defects including impaired microtubule bundles, shorter interkinetochore distance, and increased aneuploidy.
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C16 represent established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to previous literature. These claims provide necessary context for the current work and are appropriately cited. The characterization of augmin structure and function (C11, C12, C13, C15) and depletion phenotypes (C14) are well-established in the field.

result: Prior work has linked augmin depletion to segregation errors, lagging chromosomes, impaired brain development, and cancer. Augmin depletion has been linked to higher incidence of segregation errors and lagging chromosomes, which were connected to impaired brain development. Homozygous loss of HAUS6 was observed in several cancer types including sarcomas, pancreatic adenocarcinomas, gliomas, and glioblastomas.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19 are supported by appropriate citations to previous work (Wu et al., 2008; Almeida et al., 2022; Viais et al., 2021) and cancer genomics databases (ICGC/TCGA via cBioPortal). These claims provide important context for the clinical relevance of the findings.

result: Most midplane-crossing microtubules start at different points along the k-fiber, with minus ends found less than 50 nm from the k-fiber wall at distances 2-4 µm from the pole in RPE1 cells.
evaluation: Claims C83 and C84 are supported by citations to electron microscopy and electron tomography studies (Mastronarde et al., 1993; O'Toole et al., 2020). These provide important structural context supporting the augmin-dependent nucleation model.

result: Prior work on interkinetochore tension and checkpoint function. Treatment with microtubule-destabilizing agents that thin k-fibers reduces interkinetochore tension, and similar effects are observed upon PRC1 depletion. Augmin-depleted cells with compromised bridging fibers have extensive mitotic delays, suggesting bridging fibers may be important for checkpoint silencing.
evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by appropriate citations to previous work (Dudka et al., 2018; Jagrić et al., 2021; Kajtez et al., 2016; Polak et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2008). These provide important context for interpreting the tension measurements and checkpoint bypass experiments in the current study.

result: Speculation on clinical relevance and error correction mechanisms. Proteins involved in bridging fiber nucleation and crosslinking (HAUS6, HAUS8, PRC1) have been linked to various cancers, suggesting impairment of bridging fibers may contribute to aneuploidy in cancers. Lagging chromosomes following augmin depletion had reduced interkinetochore distance consistent with 'lazy chromosomes.' Bridging fibers may serve as tracks guiding Aurora B to kinetochores for error correction.
evaluation: Claims C90-C92 represent speculative connections and hypotheses. While C90 is supported by cancer genomics data citations, the causal connection to aneuploidy is speculative. C91 is supported by data from the current study and citations, but C92 is explicitly speculative, citing only a preprint. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not directly tested in the current manuscript.

result: K-fibers in RPE1 cells consist of 12.6±1.7 microtubules based on electron tomography.
evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by citation to an electron tomography study (O'Toole et al., 2020). This value is used as a reference for calculating the number of microtubules in bridging fibers and serves as a critical parameter for the quantitative analysis.
